lessons.subject: Mathematics
lessons.title: Multiply by ten
lessons.goal: Use place value to explain multiplication of a two-digit number by 10.
lessons.explanation: Twenty-four groups of ten equal 240; each ones unit becomes ten times as large.

steps: Represent 24 as 2 tens and 4 ones.
Scale each group tenfold: 20×10=200 and 4×10=40.
Combine 200+40=240; compare with 24 equal ten-bundles.

materials: Pencil-drawn number cards or locally available counters
steps: Model the worked calculation with equal groups or an area drawing.
Explain each step and why the method conserves the correct number of objects.
Solve the independent problem and check with a second representation.

independent.feedback: Twenty-four groups of ten equal 240; each ones unit becomes ten times as large.

lessons.remedial: Do not rely on writing a zero without explaining why the places change.
lessons.revision: Explain the group size, number of groups, and how the same result can be represented another way.
lessons.teacher: Ask the learner how they know the answer makes sense; check equal-groups meaning and representation.

visual.brief: Two base-ten groups and four one-unit groups scaled by ten.

lessons.subject: Mathematics
lessons.title: Multiply by multiples of ten
lessons.goal: Multiply a two-digit number by 20, 30 or 40 using factorisation.
lessons.explanation: Twenty-three groups of thirty mean 23 × (3 × 10). First 23 × 3 gives 69, then 69 tens make 690. The value of each ten-bundle is preserved.

steps: Rewrite 30 as 3×10.
Multiply 69 by ten to get 690 and check an approximate result.

materials: Pencil-drawn number cards or locally available counters
steps: Model the worked calculation with equal groups or an area drawing.
Explain each step and why the method conserves the correct number of objects.
Solve the independent problem and check with a second representation.

lessons.remedial: Treat the factor 30 as three tens, not simply three.
lessons.revision: Explain the group size, number of groups, and how the same result can be represented another way.
lessons.teacher: Ask the learner how they know the answer makes sense; check equal-groups meaning and representation.

visual.brief: Twenty-three bundles each containing three tens.

lessons.subject: Mathematics
lessons.title: Two-digit factors without regrouping
lessons.explanation: 32×12=32×(10+2)=320+64=384, because the tens and ones parts cover the whole rectangle.

steps: Split 12 into ten and two.
Calculate 32×10=320 and 32×2=64.
Join 320+64=384 and verify on an area model.

materials: Pencil-drawn number cards or locally available counters
steps: Model the worked calculation with equal groups or an area drawing.
Explain each step and why the method conserves the correct number of objects.
Solve the independent problem and check with a second representation.

independent.feedback: 32×12=32×(10+2)=320+64=384, because the tens and ones parts cover the whole rectangle.

lessons.remedial: Avoid treating the tens digit of 12 as one unit.
lessons.revision: Explain the group size, number of groups, and how the same result can be represented another way.
lessons.teacher: Ask the learner how they know the answer makes sense; check equal-groups meaning and representation.

lessons.subject: Mathematics
lessons.title: Two-digit multiplication with regrouping
lessons.goal: Explain exchanging ten ones for a ten while multiplying.

steps: Partition 13 as ten and three.
Calculate 24×3=72 using 4×3=12 and exchange ten ones for one ten.
Add 24×10=240 to 72 for a total of 312.

materials: Pencil-drawn number cards or locally available counters
steps: Model the worked calculation with equal groups or an area drawing.
Explain each step and why the method conserves the correct number of objects.
Solve the independent problem and check with a second representation.

lessons.remedial: The 1 in 13 represents one ten; 24×1 is not the tens partial product.
lessons.revision: Explain the group size, number of groups, and how the same result can be represented another way.
lessons.teacher: Ask the learner how they know the answer makes sense; check equal-groups meaning and representation.

visual.brief: Area model with 24×10 and 24×3; label the exchange.

lessons.subject: Mathematics
lessons.title: Estimate products using nearest tens
lessons.goal: Round two factors to nearest tens and estimate a product not exceeding 1,000.
lessons.explanation: 24 rounds to 20 and 36 to 40; 20×40=800, close to the exact product 864.

steps: Round 24 to 20 because 4 is below 5.
Round 36 to 40 because 6 is at least 5.
Compute estimated 20×40=800 and compare with exact 864.

materials: Pencil-drawn number cards or locally available counters
steps: Model the worked calculation with equal groups or an area drawing.
Explain each step and why the method conserves the correct number of objects.
Solve the independent problem and check with a second representation.

independent.feedback: 24 rounds to 20 and 36 to 40; 20×40=800, close to the exact product 864.

lessons.remedial: An estimate is approximate; do not label the unrounded product as the estimate.
lessons.revision: Explain the group size, number of groups, and how the same result can be represented another way.
lessons.teacher: Ask the learner how they know the answer makes sense; check equal-groups meaning and representation.

lessons.subject: Mathematics
lessons.title: Recognise multiplication patterns
lessons.goal: Build and extend multiples-based patterns, with products at most 100.
lessons.explanation: Each additional group of twelve adds twelve more, producing 12, 24, 36, 48 and 60.

steps: Start with one group of 12.
Add one equal group each time to make 12,24,36,48,60.
Check all differences are +12 and all products are at most 100.

materials: Pencil-drawn number cards or locally available counters
steps: Model the worked calculation with equal groups or an area drawing.
Explain each step and why the method conserves the correct number of objects.
Solve the independent problem and check with a second representation.

independent.prompt: Find all products for 9 multiplied by 2, 3, 4, 5
independent.feedback: Each additional group of twelve adds twelve more, producing 12, 24, 36, 48 and 60.

lessons.remedial: Add a constant group amount rather than multiplying the previous term.
lessons.revision: Explain the group size, number of groups, and how the same result can be represented another way.
lessons.teacher: Ask the learner how they know the answer makes sense; check equal-groups meaning and representation.

lessons.subject: Mathematics
lessons.title: Create a multiplication pattern
lessons.goal: Create a pattern that follows a multiplication table and prove its step.
lessons.explanation: Increasing the second factor by one adds eight to each product, yielding 24,32,40,48,56.

steps: Write 8×3 through 8×7.
Find products 24,32,40,48,56.
Check each adjacent difference equals eight and stays at most 100.

materials: Pencil-drawn number cards or locally available counters
steps: Model the worked calculation with equal groups or an area drawing.
Explain each step and why the method conserves the correct number of objects.
Solve the independent problem and check with a second representation.

independent.prompt: Find all products for 7 multiplied by 3, 4, 5, 6
independent.feedback: Increasing the second factor by one adds eight to each product, yielding 24,32,40,48,56.

lessons.remedial: Use equal groups to confirm the multiplier increases by exactly one.
lessons.revision: Explain the group size, number of groups, and how the same result can be represented another way.
lessons.teacher: Ask the learner how they know the answer makes sense; check equal-groups meaning and representation.

lessons.subject: Mathematics
lessons.title: Use multiplication in everyday planning
lessons.goal: Choose multiplication to solve an equal-groups word problem and label units.
lessons.explanation: Twenty-four rows with twelve seedlings each contain 24×12=288 seedlings; repeated addition gives the same total.

steps: Identify 24 equal rows containing 12 seedlings each.
Combine to 288 seedlings; compare with a reasonable estimate.

materials: Pencil-drawn number cards or locally available counters
steps: Model the worked calculation with equal groups or an area drawing.
Explain each step and why the method conserves the correct number of objects.
Solve the independent problem and check with a second representation.

independent.feedback: Twenty-four rows with twelve seedlings each contain 24×12=288 seedlings; repeated addition gives the same total.

lessons.remedial: If the learner adds the two factors, explain why equal groups require repeated addition or multiplication.
lessons.revision: Explain the group size, number of groups, and how the same result can be represented another way.
lessons.teacher: Ask the learner how they know the answer makes sense; check equal-groups meaning and representation.
